summary_html: Case results in **child fatality or serious injury**, triggering mandatory federal and state review. Data and lessons inform systemic reform.
authority_html:

- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure and case review of fatalities

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Little v. Utah State Division of Family Services
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed a judgment against the Division of Family Services for the death of an autistic child in a foster home, holding that although the decision to place a child may be discretionary, once placement occurs the agency owes and can be held to an ordinary duty of due care in supervising that placement.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Utah authority permitting recovery when a child dies from inadequate supervision of a state-arranged placement.
key_cases.quote: the question was no longer whether the child was to receive foster care but whether due care was exercised under a duty assumed

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed summary judgment for the State on the ground of duty rather than immunity, holding that corrections and supervision officials owed no duty of care to a member of the general public killed by a released offender absent a specific relationship to that individual.
key_cases.relevance: It defines when a death cannot be laid at the agency's door, and so bounds Utah's fatality-liability doctrine.
key_cases.quote: we agree with the trial court's conclusion that no defendant had a duty of care toward the victim

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a State to protect a child from private violence, even where the agency knew of the danger, absent a custodial or other special relationship that the State itself created.
key_cases.relevance: It bars most federal constitutional claims after a child dies in the home, channeling such claims into state tort law like Little and Ferree.
key_cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

extended_foster_care_age: To age 21, only while the juvenile court orders DCFS to keep serving the young adult (Utah Code 80-1-102(56)(b)(i); 78A-6-120(1)(a)). A young adult who is 18 or older but younger than 21 and in DCFS custody on abuse, neglect, or dependency grounds may petition the juvenile court to be removed from division custody, and the court reviews that petition within 14 days; if removed, the young adult may petition within 90 days to re-enter division custody, and the juvenile court shall order the division to take custody (Utah Code 80-3-503)
